## Three questions {#overview}

::: {style="margin-top:110px;font-size:52px;line-height:1.4"}
- What can agentic systems accomplish now?
- What engineering constraints emerge from these systems?
- Which kinds of scientific labor scale under these constraints?
:::

::: notes
The arc moves from shared capabilities to engineering practice and then the personal choice
of what scientific practice should become. Leave the tension about agency implicit.
The tutorial offers a window into practical experience so people can make their own choices.
Cail usually finds this work very fun and enjoyable; it involves a different framing of work.
:::

</div>
</div>
</div>
</div>
</div>

::: notes
Scratch space: first explain that the axis is how long a human expert takes on tasks an agent
can complete with 50% reliability. It is not the agent's runtime. Mythos is near the suite's
measurement ceiling. The axes stay fixed. The sidebar first asks about human expert time for
a Millennium Prize Problem; advance once to replace the question with both case studies.
Cail's question: how long would a human need for a 50% chance of solving Navier–Stokes in 2026?
There is no measured human baseline. This motivates asking whether the individual-task framing
still captures what coordinated systems accomplish, rather than treating the case studies as
new METR measurements. The upper-right agent wall-time axis explicitly distinguishes these
case durations from the human-expert-time metric on the left.
88 × 10,000 = 880,000 is a constant-concurrency illustration, not measured agent-hours or human
work. The $6.5M is output-only pricing arithmetic, not actual disclosed internal cost.
Cail's possible HF joke: “they committed at least one felony.” This is a rhetorical joke, not
an established legal finding. The substantive point is the chain from a restricted environment
through multiple exploits into major machine-learning dataset infrastructure.
:::

## Yesterday’s frontier costs pennies today {#costs}

<div style="margin-top:45px">
<div style="font-size:42px;margin-bottom:40px">Navier–Stokes: 130B output tokens ≈ <strong>$6.5M</strong> at retail</div>
<div class="fragment cost-reveal" data-fragment-index="0">
<div class="cost-stage cost-left" style="font-size:30px;color:#7A6F5C">ARC-AGI-1 · semi-private evaluation</div>
<div class="cost-comparison">
<div class="cost-stage cost-left"><div style="font-size:38px">o3-preview · December 2024</div><div style="font-size:110px;color:#BC4538">$4,560</div><div style="font-size:36px">per task · 87.5%</div></div>
<div class="cost-stage cost-arrow" style="font-size:70px">→</div>
<div class="cost-stage cost-right"><div style="font-size:38px">DeepSeek-V4-Flash · July 2026</div><div style="font-size:110px;color:#3F8278">$0.021</div><div style="font-size:36px">per task · 87.0%</div></div>
</div>


</div>
<details style="font-size:28px;color:#7A6F5C;margin-top:24px;max-height:170px;overflow:auto"><summary style="cursor:pointer">Sources &amp; accounting notes</summary>
<p><a href="https://arcprize.org/blog/oai-o3-pub-breakthrough">ARC Prize: o3 score &amp; retrospective cost</a> · <a href="https://arcprize.org/results/deepseek-v4-flash-0731">ARC Prize: DeepSeek score &amp; cost</a> · <a href="https://openai.com/index/navier-stokes-solution/">OpenAI: Navier–Stokes token count</a> · <a href="https://x.com/deredleritt3r/status/2098527713002672152">Prompted by prinz</a></p>
<p>ARC-AGI-1 semi-private evaluation; different systems and inference budgets. o3’s $4,560 is a retrospective estimate using o3-pro pricing. DeepSeek High: 87.0% at $0.021402901/task.</p>
<p><a href="https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/models/gpt-6-astra">Astra retail output price: $50/M</a>. Navier–Stokes: 130B output tokens × $50/M = $6.5M, output-only retail equivalent, not disclosed internal spend. The benchmark comparison does not predict future Navier–Stokes cost.</p>
</details>
</div>

::: notes
The comparison is near-equal performance on the same ARC-AGI-1 semi-private benchmark category,
with different models and inference budgets. ARC retrospectively estimated the o3 high-compute
cost using o3-pro pricing in December 2025; this is not an actual December 2024 bill.
DeepSeek's High configuration scored 87.0% at $0.021402901/task. The cost ratio is about 213,000.
This motivates distinguishing the cost of demonstrating a capability from its later deployment
cost. It does not establish when an open model could solve Navier–Stokes, in how much time, or
at what cost. The tweet's 2028 prediction remains its author's speculation.
Navier pricing is a separate illustration, not a forecast or disclosed internal spend.
:::

## What does this mean for scaling our personal research? {#engineering-bridge}

```{=html}
<div class="engineering-analogy">
<div class="r-stack">
<ul class="fragment fade-out" data-fragment-index="0">
<li>Agentic approaches can solve hard scientific problems.</li>
<li>Certain kinds of scientific labor will scale with tokens.</li>
<li>Tokens at fixed capabilities get cheaper, intensifying this scaling.</li>
</ul>
<ul class="fragment fade-in" data-fragment-index="0">
<li><strong>Computational</strong> approaches can solve hard scientific problems.</li>
<li>Certain kinds of scientific labor will scale with <strong>computation</strong>.</li>
<li><strong>Computation</strong> at fixed capabilities gets cheaper, intensifying this scaling.</li>
</ul>
</div>
<div class="fragment historical-computer" data-fragment-index="0">Imagine being a “computer” in the 1950s…</div>
</div>
```

<details><summary>Sources &amp; notes</summary>

[NASA: Langley’s human computers, 1935–1970](https://www.nasa.gov/history/langleys-computers-1935-1970/). The transition was gradual; some human computers took on programming duties, and the job title persisted into the 1960s. This is an analogy about changing work, not an exact forecast of displacement.

</details>

::: notes
One advance replaces the agentic formulation with the computational analogy, leading into
how computing changed physics and astronomy. This is an argument about work we can organize
to benefit from additional resources, not a claim that every task scales with token count.
Cheaper tokens at comparable capability are a premise for the outlook, not a guaranteed price
trajectory. Both versions use “fixed capabilities”; only agentic/computational and tokens/computation change.
The next slides make the engineering constraints concrete; adoption remains a personal choice.
Cail’s spoken analogy: computing transformed existing subdomains of physics and astronomy,
and new subdomains emerged from the new constraints. Keep this explanation off the slide.
The following slide introduces emerging practices and the invitation to explore them.
:::

## A roadmap for the rest of the talk {#roadmap}

<div class="talk-roadmap">
<div><span class="roadmap-number">01</span><span>Emerging building blocks</span></div>
<div><span class="roadmap-number">02</span><span>A live demo: a small scientific analysis</span></div>
<div><span class="roadmap-number">03</span><span>High-level strategies</span></div>
</div>
<div class="roadmap-choice fragment" data-fragment-index="0">
<div>To inform your own research practice:</div>
<ul><li>Do you <strong>want</strong> to work this way?</li><li>If you do, which parts do you want to scale?</li></ul>
</div>

::: notes
The remaining talk has three parts: emerging low-level concepts, a live agentic analysis,
and higher-level ways of organizing research. The purpose is informed choice, not a demand
to adopt these tools. Give people a window into practical experience, then enough conceptual
grounding to reason about their own practice: whether to engage, which labor to scale,
and which activities to keep doing themselves. Both choices are legitimate.
:::

::: notes
This single slide replaces the previous four-slide computing/history/constraints sequence.
The left names established software-engineering concepts. Their paths mix and dissolve into
a shared fog: the new categories and their relationships are not yet settled. Do not label
the right side or imply a one-to-one mapping. The coming primitives provide
concrete partial answers: intent and specifications, harnesses, context and durable memory,
verification, and orchestration. Computing transformed existing fields and created new ones.
The optimistic opportunity is both more ambitious science and room to invent a research
practice. Keep that spoken rather than adding another slogan. Adoption is an informed choice.
:::

<div style="font-size:40px;margin-top:25px">Standard context length: 1M tokens</div>

```{=html}
</g>
</svg>
```

::: notes
Context is a finite working set, analogous to RAM. Show the session's accumulating sequence:
system prompt, user messages, model responses and tool results. Empty capacity stays unlabeled.
First advance: a read tool returns file contents, occupying context. The malloc analogy is
about consuming a finite working budget, not literal allocation: tokens are not addressable RAM,
and reading generally appends content rather than reserving an independently freeable block.
Second advance: compaction summarizes the history into a fresh model context after the system
prompt. This can continue the same user-facing session; it need not create a new chat.
The drawing is schematic: implementations may preserve recent turns and tool state as well.
Summarization is lossy. Keep consequential decisions and evidence in durable files.
:::

<details><summary>Sources &amp; notes</summary>
<p><a href="https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/prompt-caching">OpenAI: prompt caching</a> (animation adapted from “What is the prompt cache?”); <a href="https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/pricing#text-tokens">OpenAI pricing</a>; <a href="https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/about-claude/pricing">Claude pricing</a>; <a href="https://x.com/trq212/status/2024574133011673516">Thariq: Prompt Caching Is Everything</a>.</p>
<p>Rates checked September 17, 2026. Astra and Fable 5.1 both have $10/M base input, $12.50/M short-cache writes and $50/M output; cache reads are $1/M and $0.25/M respectively. Astra: standard short-context API pricing. Fable: five-minute cache writes; one-hour writes cost $20/M. Read multipliers are 0.1× and 0.025× respectively; output 5×. Prices exclude batch, fast mode, regional uplifts and other modifiers.</p>
<p>Illustrative Astra short-context accounting: Turn 1 writes a 100k-token prefix ($1.25) and generates 20k output tokens ($1). Turn 2 hits the original 100k ($0.10), writes the previous 20k-token answer ($0.25) plus a 4k-token user follow-up ($0.05), and generates another 20k ($1). Turn 5 continues the same pattern: its cached prefix is 100k + 3 × 24k = 172k tokens ($0.172), followed by the latest 20k-token assistant answer ($0.25 write), a 4k-token user addition ($0.05 write), and 20k output ($1). Turns 3–4 are omitted; each adds 24k tokens to the next cached prefix. All bars share a linear scale of 6.02 SVG units per 1,000 tokens. The initial prefix consists of 96k instructions/tool tokens and a 4k user message; arrows are fixed separators, not tokens. The example assumes the indicated cache hits; actual reusable boundaries depend on the service. Fable 5.1 read costs are one quarter of these Astra read costs. KV states, not a ready-made answer, are cached.</p>
<p>Retention is model-specific: Astra's documented minimum is 30 minutes after write/reuse; Claude offers five-minute and one-hour writes. Older OpenAI in-memory caches typically last 5–10 minutes of inactivity, up to one hour.</p>
</details>

::: notes
Stay at conversation-turn level. First show instructions, tools and the user's message being processed, followed by an answer. Advance: retain that prefix, append the answer and follow-up, and generate another answer. Cache reuse avoids reprocessing the matched history; new history and output still cost money. The boundary is schematic, not a promise that output is never cached. Final reveal gives representative multipliers relative to $10/M base input; exact per-model rates stay in Sources & notes. KV mechanics are supporting detail, not the on-slide explanation.
:::

## Delegate to sub-agents for scoped work {#delegation}

```{=html}
<svg class="delegation-schematic" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 1600 680" style="width:100%;margin-top:40px" font-family="EB Garamond,Georgia,serif">
<path d="M235 300 H535" fill="none" stroke="#C5B89E" stroke-width="3"/><circle cx="160" cy="300" r="75" fill="#FBF6E9" stroke="#BC4538" stroke-width="3"/><text x="160" y="312" text-anchor="middle" font-size="36" fill="#BC4538">You</text><circle cx="620" cy="300" r="85" fill="#FBF6E9" stroke="#3F8278" stroke-width="3"/><text x="620" y="312" text-anchor="middle" font-size="36" fill="#3F8278">Agent</text><g class="fragment"><path d="M705 300 Q900 300 1075 130" fill="none" stroke="#C5B89E" stroke-width="3"/><circle cx="1150" cy="130" r="75" fill="#FBF6E9" stroke="#3D5BA0" stroke-width="3"/><text x="1150" y="142" text-anchor="middle" font-size="36" fill="#3D5BA0">Sub-agent</text></g><text x="800" y="603" text-anchor="middle" font-size="37"><tspan fill="#1B1611">Useful pattern: </tspan><tspan fill="#3F8278">strong model for discussion and planning</tspan></text>
<text x="800" y="650" text-anchor="middle" font-size="37" fill="#3D5BA0">sub-agent for scoped exploration and implementation</text>
</svg>
```

::: notes
Start with user → main agent → tools. Advance adds a bounded worker with its own context. Examples include literature search, code investigation, review, and implementation. The main session carries the relationship with the user and integrates the result. Delegation is not necessarily parallel, and a returned summary is not proof of correctness. Separate context does not always mean a fork: Claude Code supports both full-history forks and fresh-context agents. This Codex session can inherit all, some, or none of the conversation. Two use cases: an independent side investigation, or a conversational lead delegating implementation and exploration. Model-cost allocation belongs on the following teams slide.
:::

## Teams coordinate while the work is happening {#agent-teams}

```{=html}
<svg class="delegation-schematic" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 1600 680" style="width:100%;margin-top:40px" font-family="EB Garamond,Georgia,serif">
<path d="M235 300 H535" fill="none" stroke="#C5B89E" stroke-width="3"/><circle cx="160" cy="300" r="75" fill="#FBF6E9" stroke="#BC4538" stroke-width="3"/><text x="160" y="312" text-anchor="middle" font-size="36" fill="#BC4538">You</text><circle cx="620" cy="300" r="85" fill="#FBF6E9" stroke="#3F8278" stroke-width="3"/><text x="620" y="312" text-anchor="middle" font-size="36" fill="#3F8278">Lead</text><path d="M705 300 Q900 300 1075 130" fill="none" stroke="#C5B89E" stroke-width="3"/><circle cx="1150" cy="130" r="75" fill="#FBF6E9" stroke="#3D5BA0" stroke-width="3"/><text x="1150" y="142" text-anchor="middle" font-size="36" fill="#3D5BA0">Search</text><circle class="team-message" r="9" fill="#3F8278">
<animateMotion dur="6s" begin="0s" repeatCount="indefinite" path="M705 300 Q900 300 1075 130" keyPoints="0;1;1;0;0" keyTimes="0;0.4;0.5;0.9;1" calcMode="linear"/>
<animate attributeName="fill" values="#3F8278;#3D5BA0;#3F8278" keyTimes="0;0.5;1" calcMode="discrete" dur="6s" begin="0s" repeatCount="indefinite"/>
</circle><path d="M705 300 H1255" fill="none" stroke="#C5B89E" stroke-width="3"/><circle cx="1330" cy="300" r="75" fill="#FBF6E9" stroke="#3D5BA0" stroke-width="3"/><text x="1330" y="312" text-anchor="middle" font-size="36" fill="#3D5BA0">Build</text><circle class="team-message" r="9" fill="#3F8278">
<animateMotion dur="6s" begin="-2s" repeatCount="indefinite" path="M705 300 H1255" keyPoints="0;1;1;0;0" keyTimes="0;0.4;0.5;0.9;1" calcMode="linear"/>
<animate attributeName="fill" values="#3F8278;#3D5BA0;#3F8278" keyTimes="0;0.5;1" calcMode="discrete" dur="6s" begin="-2s" repeatCount="indefinite"/>
</circle><path d="M705 300 Q900 300 1025 500" fill="none" stroke="#C5B89E" stroke-width="3"/><circle cx="1100" cy="500" r="75" fill="#FBF6E9" stroke="#3D5BA0" stroke-width="3"/><text x="1100" y="512" text-anchor="middle" font-size="36" fill="#3D5BA0">Review</text><circle class="team-message" r="9" fill="#3F8278">
<animateMotion dur="6s" begin="-4s" repeatCount="indefinite" path="M705 300 Q900 300 1025 500" keyPoints="0;1;1;0;0" keyTimes="0;0.4;0.5;0.9;1" calcMode="linear"/>
<animate attributeName="fill" values="#3F8278;#3D5BA0;#3F8278" keyTimes="0;0.5;1" calcMode="discrete" dur="6s" begin="-4s" repeatCount="indefinite"/>
</circle><circle class="team-message" r="9" fill="#BC4538">
<animateMotion dur="6s" begin="-1s" repeatCount="indefinite" path="M235 300 H535" keyPoints="0;1;1;0;0" keyTimes="0;0.4;0.5;0.9;1" calcMode="linear"/>
<animate attributeName="fill" values="#BC4538;#3F8278;#BC4538" keyTimes="0;0.5;1" calcMode="discrete" dur="6s" begin="-1s" repeatCount="indefinite"/>
</circle><text x="800" y="635" text-anchor="middle" font-size="40" fill="#1B1611">Models now trained in multi-agent environments…</text></svg>
```

::: notes
Message motion illustrates ongoing communication, not real telemetry. The lead can clarify scope, interrupt, redirect, and integrate emerging results; some systems also support peer messaging. This differs from fire-and-forget delegation. Shared goals, ownership, and communication discipline are necessary: more messages do not automatically mean better coordination. Preserve the user’s ability to steer. A strong, expensive lead can concentrate judgment in design and decomposition, giving lower-cost workers sufficiently clear task parameters. Model choice should follow task difficulty: review and ambiguous research can still need frontier intelligence. This is a useful allocation pattern, not a guarantee of lower total cost.
:::

## Workflows express loops and parallelism on the fly {#generated-workflow}

## With great output comes great chaos {#experiment-record}

```{=html}
<svg viewBox="0 0 1600 650" style="width:100%;max-height:730px;margin-top:45px" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" font-family="EB Garamond,Georgia,serif" role="img" aria-label="A slop cannon scatters notebooks, scripts, plots and incompatible results. An analysis record reconnects inputs, choices and outputs.">
<defs><g id="slop-page"><path d="M0 0 H125 L155 30 V140 H0 Z M125 0 V30 H155" fill="#FBF6E9" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2.5"/></g></defs>
<path d="M100 560 H780" stroke="#C5B89E" stroke-width="2"/>
<g transform="translate(140 365) rotate(-19)"><path d="M0 0 Q-45 65 0 125 L300 125 V0 Z" fill="#C5B89E" stroke="#1B1611" stroke-width="4"/><ellipse cx="300" cy="62" rx="24" ry="64" fill="#1B1611"/><ellipse cx="300" cy="62" rx="12" ry="47" fill="#7A6F5C"/><path d="M25 15 H265 M25 108 H265" stroke="#7A6F5C" stroke-width="3"/><text x="136" y="78" font-size="36" text-anchor="middle" fill="#1B1611">SLOP</text></g>
<path d="M195 450 L145 540 H365 L300 430" fill="#7A6F5C" stroke="#1B1611" stroke-width="3"/><circle cx="250" cy="514" r="48" fill="#FBF6E9" stroke="#1B1611" stroke-width="5"/><circle cx="250" cy="514" r="9" fill="#1B1611"/><path d="M250 466 V562 M202 514 H298 M216 480 L284 548 M216 548 L284 480" stroke="#1B1611" stroke-width="2"/>
<path d="M443 308 l40 -32 m-14 65 l42 -6 m-79 -64 l5 -40" stroke="#BC4538" stroke-width="5" stroke-linecap="round"/>
<g transform="translate(530 95) rotate(-16)" color="#3D5BA0"><use href="#slop-page"/><text x="15" y="65" font-size="28" fill="currentColor">fit_v7.py</text><path d="M18 87 H100 M18 102 H125 M18 117 H80" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="3"/></g>
<g transform="translate(740 210) rotate(17)" color="#BC4538"><use href="#slop-page"/><path d="M22 112 V48 M22 112 H129 M30 97 L49 87 L65 96 L87 57 L105 69 L122 40" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="3"/></g>
<g transform="translate(495 392) rotate(13)" color="#7A6F5C"><use href="#slop-page"/><text x="13" y="62" font-size="28" fill="currentColor">final_final</text><text x="13" y="99" font-size="28" fill="currentColor">.ipynb</text></g>
<g transform="translate(780 435) rotate(-11)" color="#3F8278"><use href="#slop-page"/><text x="15" y="65" font-size="28" fill="currentColor">chain.npy</text><path d="M16 91 H129 M16 108 H129" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"/></g>
<text x="545" y="620" font-size="36" fill="#BC4538" text-anchor="middle">100 files from 20 experiments</text>
<path d="M990 55 V590" stroke="#C5B89E" stroke-width="2"/>
<text x="1300" y="105" text-anchor="middle" font-size="40" fill="#1B1611">What belongs together?</text>
<g font-size="37"><text x="1080" y="240" fill="#3D5BA0">Inputs</text><text x="1080" y="338" fill="#BC4538">Decisions</text><text x="1080" y="436" fill="#3F8278">Recipe → outputs</text></g>
<path d="M1050 207 H1032 V448 H1050" fill="none" stroke="#7A6F5C" stroke-width="3"/>

</svg>
```

::: notes
The slop cannon is a joke about unorganized throughput, not a claim that every generated artifact is worthless. Growing work can mix incompatible inputs, configurations, and outputs. Naming files is useful but insufficient: record which inputs, decisions, recipes, and outputs belong to each analysis. This motivates ASTRA without claiming a schema eliminates every provenance error. Distinguish remembering why a decision was made from validating that the current run used it.
:::

## Live Demo: Measure Dark Energy in 15 Minutes {#tutorial-open}

```{=html}
<div class="candle-demo">
<div style="font-size:38px;text-align:center;line-height:1.45;margin-top:15px">Supernovae are standard candles:</div>
<svg id="candle-plot" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 1600 620" style="width:100%;height:620px" font-family="EB Garamond,Georgia,serif" role="img" aria-label="Standard candles on a distance–redshift plot, with a flat LCDM prediction controlled by Omega Lambda">
<defs><radialGradient id="candle-glow"><stop offset="0" stop-color="#FFC857" stop-opacity=".8"/><stop offset="1" stop-color="#FFC857" stop-opacity="0"/></radialGradient></defs>
<g id="candle-axes"></g>
<path id="candle-prediction" fill="none" stroke="#3F8278" stroke-width="5"/>
<g id="candle-observations"></g>
<text x="850" y="605" text-anchor="middle" font-size="36">Redshift (cosmic expansion)</text>
<text transform="translate(75 300) rotate(-90)" text-anchor="middle" font-size="36">Distance (from brightness)</text>
</svg>
<div style="display:flex;align-items:center;justify-content:center;gap:30px;font-size:40px;color:#3F8278"><label for="candle-omega">ΩΛ</label><input id="candle-omega" aria-label="Omega Lambda" type="range" min="0" max="1" step="0.01" value="0.7" style="width:650px;accent-color:#3F8278"></div>
</div>
```

::: notes
Type Ia supernovae are standardizable candles. Their calibrated luminosity and apparent brightness give luminosity distance. Spectra give redshift; the distance–redshift relation constrains expansion history. The candles stay fixed as the model prediction changes. The tutorial uses actual Union2.1 measurements to fit Omega_Lambda.
:::

```{.bash code-line-numbers="false"}

export PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH"
```

```{.bash code-line-numbers="false"}

```

```{.bash code-line-numbers="false"}

```
**Codex**


<details><summary>Sources &amp; notes</summary>

[uv installer](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/getting-started/installation/) · [Lightcone plugins](https://github.com/LightconeResearch/agent-skills)

The CLI block creates and enters `/tmp/lightcone-demo`, reusing it if it already exists. Run the setup and your chosen agent in the same terminal. Copy out results you want to keep before the operating system clears temporary files. The uv installer and CLI use their standard user-level installation locations. The CLI includes astra-tools; the Lightcone plugin bundles ASTRA guidance and hooks. Start a fresh agent session after installation. Create the analysis with prompt 1 before opening JupyterLab.

</details>


## 1. Kick off an analysis with Lightcone {#step-spec}

::: {.live-pair}
::: {.live-left}
::: {.prompt-card}
I'd like to use Lightcone tools to analyze the Union2.1 supernova compilation from the Supernova Cosmology Project. Let's write an ASTRA analysis that fits a flat LCDM model to this data and recovers Omega_Lambda.

Please produce two outputs: the best fit Omega_Lambda with uncertainties, and a downstream Hubble diagram figure with an absolute panel and a residuals panel. As you go, briefly walk me through each ASTRA element that you add; this is a live tutorial! Don't add any decisions yet.

<a class="prompt-source" data-copy-url href="https://supernova.lbl.gov/Union/figures/SCPUnion2.1_mu_vs_z.txt">Union2.1 catalogue ↗</a>
:::
:::
::: {.live-right}
::: {.watch-head}
while it runs — an illustrative spec
:::
```yaml
inputs:
  - id: union21
    type: data
    source: data/union21.txt

outputs:
  - id: best_fit
    type: metric
    inputs: [union21]
    recipe:
      command: python fit.py …
  - id: hubble_diagram
    type: figure
    inputs: [union21, best_fit]
    recipe:
      command: python plot.py …
```
:::
:::

::: notes
Step one: say what the analysis is, in words, and the agent writes the spec. Inputs: the data file.
Outputs: a best-fit — Omega Lambda with uncertainty, chi-squared — and a Hubble-diagram figure
downstream of it. Each output carries a recipe: the exact command that produces it, with the
dependencies explicit. Notice what this is: it's a DAG again! — but look who drew it. You said four
sentences of intent; the model wrote the graph, and a hook validated the file the moment it was
saved. The graph didn't disappear from science — provenance still wants a graph — it moved from
being the thing you hand-wire to being an artifact the agent maintains.
:::

If prompt 1 created a project subdirectory, enter that directory first. These commands do not create a second temporary workspace. Both Claude Code and Codex ACP adapters are installed; continue using the terminal agent if preferred.

The tutorial sequence is agent setup → prompt 1 creates the analysis → open the project in
JupyterLab → inspect outputs → prompt 2 → prompt 3. Jupyter is a viewer and optional chat surface,
not a prerequisite for starting the analysis. Launch it from the actual ASTRA project root.

## 2. Did we reproduce the published result? {#step-verify}

::: {.live-pair}
::: {.live-left}
::: {.prompt-card}
The paper that published this catalogue is Suzuki et al. 2012, arXiv 1105.3470. Can we compare our Omega_Lambda to their supernova-only constraint?
:::
:::
::: {.live-right}
::: {.watch-head}
while it runs — what a verified claim looks like
:::
```yaml
prior_insights:
  suzuki_2012_result:
    claim: >
      [constraint from the paper]
      [assumptions + errors]
    evidence:
      - doi: >-
          10.48550/arXiv.1105.3470
        quote:
          exact: >
            [exact quote]
        location:
          value: "page=17"
```


:::
:::

::: notes
Step four: check it against the paper that published this catalogue — Suzuki et al. 2012. And
here's my favorite mechanism in the whole system. The agent caches the paper and records the
published constraint as a *prior insight* — a claim with evidence. The evidence is an exact quote,
with a page number — and ASTRA searches the cached PDF and verifies that the quote actually appears
on page seventeen. This matters because agents, like graduate students, occasionally remember
papers saying things they don't say. Claims about the literature are grounded in the literature,
mechanically. And with the quote verified, we can compare: they got 0.705, plus 0.040 minus 0.043.
Our central value agrees nicely. But look at the error bars — ours are three times tighter, on the
same 580 supernovae. Same data, same model. Something is wrong, and it's wrong in the direction
that should scare you: we're *too* confident.
:::


## 3. What changes when we include systematics? {#step-decision}

::: {.live-pair}
::: {.live-left}
::: {.prompt-card}
Let's improve our systematics treatment to reproduce their published result. Track all changes as ASTRA decisions.
:::
:::
::: {.live-right}
::: {.watch-head}
Choose the covariance treatment
:::
```yaml
decisions:
  covariance:
    label: Covariance treatment
    rationale: Account for systematics
    default: full
    options:
      stat_only:
        label: Statistical only
      full:
        label: Statistical + systematic

outputs:
  best_fit:
    decisions: [covariance]
    # recipe uses the selected option
```
:::
:::

::: notes
Step five, and the payoff. We ask the agent to find out why: download the two Union2.1 covariance
files — with and without systematics — work out which one our error column corresponds to, and
record a *decision* in the spec: statistical-only versus full systematic covariance. The answer:
our fit had been using the no-systematics errors — the error column in the data file *is* the diagonal
of the no-systematics covariance, to twelve decimal places. Everything the systematic covariance knows was
sitting in a file we had never opened. Switch to it, and watch the plot: the central value barely
moves — 0.722 to 0.714 — but the uncertainty more than doubles, and only then does our measurement
actually lie beside the published one: 0.2 sigma apart, their data, their systematics, their
method. Here's the lesson, and it's the sentence I'd have you take home: if you had ranked this
choice by its effect on the best-fit number, it would have looked nearly irrelevant. It is the
difference between a number that *resembles* theirs and a number you can *put beside* theirs. That
is what a decision is — and this field, all of science, is made of thousands of them, almost none
of them written down. ASTRA writes them down.
:::

```{=html}
<g font-size="32" fill="#1B1611"><text x="895" y="285" fill="#3D5BA0">[[Shear power spectrum]]</text><text x="895" y="330">“…check the binning at low ℓ…”</text><text x="895" y="370" fill="#3D5BA0">→ [[Mode-coupling checks]]</text><text x="895" y="495" fill="#3D5BA0">[[Mode-coupling checks]]</text><text x="895" y="540">“…test recovery with extended bins…”</text><text x="895" y="580" fill="#3D5BA0">← [[Shear power spectrum]]</text></g>
<path d="M1195 396 V448" stroke="#3F8278" stroke-width="2" marker-start="url(#wiki-arrow)" marker-end="url(#wiki-arrow)"/>
</g>
<g class="fragment" data-fragment-index="1" fill="none" stroke="#BC4538" stroke-width="3" stroke-dasharray="8 7"><path d="M735 315 Q800 220 865 315"/><path d="M735 520 Q800 600 865 520"/></g>
<g class="fragment" data-fragment-index="1" text-anchor="middle" font-size="35" fill="#BC4538"><text x="800" y="708">“Apply the mode-coupling binning fix</text><text x="800" y="748">we used in the multi-probe cosmology project.”</text></g>
</svg>
```

::: notes
Cail’s cross-project example: in multi-probe cosmology, extending bins to low multipoles
addressed mode-coupling bias from contributions not represented by the truncated coupling
matrix. That fix also informed the cosmic shear project. The displayed snippets are condensed
illustrations of this finding, not verbatim quotes from the project records. Reveal the second
project, then the request to retrieve and apply the earlier fix. No blinded numerical results.
:::

## Iterate on long-horizon work {#iteration}

```{=html}
<svg viewBox="0 0 1600 730" style="width:100%;margin-top:35px" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" font-family="EB Garamond,Georgia,serif" role="img" aria-label="Implementation and independent review iterate in separate contexts. Testable requirements accumulate to guide the loop, freeing attention for higher-level questions.">
<defs><marker id="iteration-arrow" markerWidth="10" markerHeight="10" refX="8" refY="5" orient="auto-start-reverse"><path d="M1 1 L8 5 L1 9" fill="none" stroke="#7A6F5C" stroke-width="1.5"/></marker></defs>
<text x="800" y="55" text-anchor="middle" font-size="44">“Check your work” → checks built into the environment</text>
<g fill="none" stroke="#7A6F5C" stroke-width="3" marker-end="url(#iteration-arrow)"><path d="M560 220 C700 120 900 120 1040 220"/><path d="M1040 340 C900 440 700 440 560 340"/></g>
<ellipse cx="430" cy="280" rx="215" ry="110" fill="#3D5BA0" fill-opacity="0.05" stroke="#3D5BA0" stroke-width="2.5"/>
<ellipse cx="1170" cy="280" rx="215" ry="110" fill="#3F8278" fill-opacity="0.05" stroke="#3F8278" stroke-width="2.5"/>
<text x="430" y="294" text-anchor="middle" font-size="44" fill="#3D5BA0">Implementation</text>
<text x="1170" y="270" text-anchor="middle" font-size="44" fill="#3F8278">Independent</text>
<text x="1170" y="320" text-anchor="middle" font-size="44" fill="#3F8278">review</text>
<text x="800" y="290" text-anchor="middle" font-size="34" fill="#7A6F5C">Separate contexts</text>
<path d="M800 535 V415" fill="none" stroke="#7A6F5C" stroke-width="2.5" marker-end="url(#iteration-arrow)"/>
<g fill="#FBF6E9" stroke="#C5B89E" stroke-width="2"><rect x="442" y="573" width="716" height="66" rx="6"/><rect x="432" y="562" width="736" height="66" rx="6"/><rect x="422" y="551" width="756" height="66" rx="6"/></g>
<text x="800" y="594" text-anchor="middle" font-size="40">Accumulate testable requirements</text>
<text x="800" y="705" text-anchor="middle" font-size="40">Focus on higher-level questions.</text>
</svg>
```

::: notes
“Check your work” becomes useful when the task and environment provide ways to evaluate it.
A workflow can separate implementation and review contexts. Separate contexts do not guarantee
unbiased judgment: models may still share systematic blind spots.
:::

```{=html}
<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 1600 790" style="width:100%;margin-top:15px" font-family="EB Garamond,Georgia,serif" role="img" aria-label="Example report layout with executive summary, two plots, verification, and open questions or decisions needed">
<rect x="20" y="15" width="1560" height="755" rx="12" fill="#FBF6E9" stroke="#C5B89E" stroke-width="2"/>
<text x="65" y="75" font-size="40" fill="#1B1611">Executive summary</text>

<g stroke="#C5B89E" stroke-width="7" stroke-linecap="round"><path d="M65 108 H1260 M65 134 H995"/></g>

<g stroke="#C5B89E" stroke-width="2" fill="none"><path d="M100 222 V435 H715 M875 222 V435 H1490"/></g>
<path d="M110 409 Q310 270 705 241" stroke="#3F8278" stroke-width="4" fill="none"/>
<g fill="#3D5BA0"><circle cx="145" cy="391" r="6"/><circle cx="235" cy="330" r="6"/><circle cx="325" cy="310" r="6"/><circle cx="415" cy="276" r="6"/><circle cx="505" cy="274" r="6"/><circle cx="595" cy="247" r="6"/><circle cx="685" cy="249" r="6"/></g>
<path d="M880 325 H1480" stroke="#3F8278" stroke-width="2" stroke-dasharray="8 6"/>
<g fill="#3D5BA0"><circle cx="910" cy="316" r="6"/><circle cx="1000" cy="342" r="6"/><circle cx="1090" cy="313" r="6"/><circle cx="1180" cy="332" r="6"/><circle cx="1270" cy="319" r="6"/><circle cx="1360" cy="335" r="6"/><circle cx="1450" cy="318" r="6"/></g>
<path d="M65 480 H1530" stroke="#C5B89E" stroke-width="2"/>
<text x="65" y="535" font-size="38">Verification</text>
<g stroke="#C5B89E" stroke-width="7" stroke-linecap="round"><path d="M65 567 H1150 M65 591 H880"/></g>
<path d="M65 620 H1530" stroke="#C5B89E" stroke-width="2"/>
<text x="65" y="673" font-size="38">Open questions / decisions needed</text>
<g stroke="#C5B89E" stroke-width="7" stroke-linecap="round"><path d="M65 707 H1040 M65 737 H795"/></g>
</svg>
```

::: notes
A report layout, not measured results. Request a real executive summary, plots side by side,
verification evidence, and open questions or decisions needed. The report should link to actual
artifacts and make failed or incomplete checks visible. Review the results rather than trusting
presentation polish.
:::

## Do you still need to read code? {#read-code}

<div style="margin-top:65px;font-size:44px;line-height:1.4">
<p style="font-size:56px;color:#3F8278;margin-bottom:45px">Sometimes!</p>
<ul style="margin:0;padding-left:45px">
<li style="margin-bottom:32px">Define the high-level design before implementation<br><span style="font-size:36px">(product requirements document, etc.)</span></li>
<li style="margin-bottom:32px">Grill the model until you understand what it does.<br>Diagrams help.</li>
<li>Core code is worth reading.</li>
</ul>
</div>

::: notes
Understand what the implementation does at a high level. Establish the design before delegating
implementation; then question the model until its explanation makes sense. Diagrams can help.
Read core code directly, especially fundamental architecture, scientific assumptions, and shared
primitives. Model explanations remain something to check against the source and behavior.
:::

## Which kinds of scientific labor scale under these constraints? {#choice}

<div style="text-align:center;font-size:46px;margin-top:45px">Not all problems are equally scalable.</div>

```{=html}
<svg viewBox="0 0 1600 700" style="width:100%;margin-top:15px" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" font-family="EB Garamond,Georgia,serif" role="img" aria-label="One current rises into a wave while curling into a sheltered eddy; contrasting work limited by data, instruments or people with work that benefits from more computation">
<defs><linearGradient id="choice-water" x1="0" x2="1"><stop offset="0" stop-color="#3D5BA0"/><stop offset="1" stop-color="#3F8278"/></linearGradient></defs>
<!-- A single body of water: a slow recirculation beside an accelerating crest. -->
<path d="M65 355 C210 340 300 395 470 390 C720 390 895 350 1030 220 C1125 125 1215 65 1320 105 C1390 133 1400 215 1345 235 C1320 245 1290 230 1295 202 C1340 253 1430 315 1535 330 L1535 480 C1190 515 785 500 450 490 C240 480 135 460 65 440 Z" fill="url(#choice-water)" opacity=".09"/>
<g fill="none" stroke="url(#choice-water)" stroke-linecap="round">
<path d="M65 355 C210 340 300 395 470 390 C720 390 895 350 1030 220 C1125 125 1215 65 1320 105 C1390 133 1400 215 1345 235 C1320 245 1290 230 1295 202" stroke-width="6"/>
<path d="M65 397 C205 380 280 428 470 430 C720 430 960 385 1120 245 C1215 165 1260 158 1295 175" stroke-width="4" opacity=".65"/>
<path d="M65 440 C230 455 320 480 510 470 C800 460 1030 450 1210 330 C1350 240 1420 335 1535 365" stroke-width="3" opacity=".4"/>
<!-- The eddy joins the same current instead of sitting in a separate panel. -->
<path d="M650 394 C535 368 540 255 410 225 C290 198 215 270 250 335 C285 395 455 405 480 320 C505 240 370 224 324 268 C275 315 354 364 411 334 C446 315 412 276 380 292" stroke-width="4"/>
<path d="M580 416 C508 410 485 397 475 380" stroke-width="3" opacity=".5"/>
</g>
<g stroke="#7A6F5C" stroke-width="2" fill="none"><path d="M365 405 V530"/><path d="M1215 300 V530"/></g>
<g fill="#1B1611" font-size="39" text-anchor="middle">
<text x="365" y="585">Work limited by data,</text><text x="365" y="632">instruments, or people</text>
<text x="1215" y="585">Verifiable work that benefits</text><text x="1215" y="632">from more computation</text>
</g>
</svg>
```

::: notes
The distinction is the bottleneck: additional machine effort can directly advance some
problems; others depend on obtaining data, building instruments, or sustained human interaction.
These are not permanent categories, nor a ranking of scientific worth. A project may contain
both. This connects the computational-tractability discussion to a personal choice about work,
without predicting a safe niche or prescribing adoption. The following DeepSeek quotation
provides one person's response to changing work, rather than a universal answer.
:::
